speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. This matter is the current $2 billion plus deficit Canada is running under the Canada-United States auto pact, with devastating consequences to the Canadian auto parts industry in particular and to the over-all economies of Pntario and Canada. Inasmuch as the government is not acting to deal with this crisis, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That this House constitute a special committee to inquire forthwith into, report upon and make recommendations with respect to the problems and difficulties of the Canadian auto and auto parts industries under the Canada-United States auto pact.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member has followed debate on this, as I am sure other hon. members have, he will realize that the issue is the inflation rates in the two countries. subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL PARTICIPATING IN PUBLIC SERVICE CLOSED COMPETITIONS
speechtext:

speechtext:
1.	Does the Department of National Revenue list OXFAM as a charitable organization and, if so, are donations tax deductible?
2.	Do liberation movements in Africa receive support from OXFAM and, if so, does the government (a) approve of each liberation organization receiving such support (b) financially support such liberation movements and, if not, is it considering giving such support?
3.	Does the government register organizations which engage in funding of political liberation movements as charitable organizations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL PARTICIPATING IN PUBLIC SERVICE CLOSED COMPETITIONS
subsubtopic: REGISTERED CANADIAN CHARITABLE ORGANIZATIONS- OXFAM
speechtext:
I am informed by the Department of National Revenue and the Canadian International Development Agency as follows; 1. OXFAM-Canada, an Ontario Part II no share capital corporation, has been registered as a Canadian charitable organization with Revenue-Canada since January 1, 1967. Accordingly, donations to it are tax deductible by the donor within the provisions of paragraph 110(1) (a) of the Income Tax Act.
2. Some liberation groups in Africa have received support from OXFAM, and OXFAM has sought financial contributions from CIDA for such assistance projects as might qualify under Canada's humanitarian aid program for

southern Africa. To date, CIDA has given financial assistance to OXFAM/Quebec for its humanitarian assistance program for the Zimbabwe African Peoples Union. This involved a grant of $5,000 to OXFAM for the purpose of sending clothing, food and medical supplies for refugees who fled from Rhodesia to neighbouring countries. At the present time CIDA is considering a request from OXFAM-Canada for assistance to the South West Africa People organization in Namibia for a project involving Adult Education, (a) The Government approves the receiving by liberation organizations of support by Canadian non-governmental organizations for humanitarian purposes. However, firm assurances are required that the aid is utilized for purely peaceful purposes involving strict accountability by sponsoring bodies for any CIDA funds. Funds are not made available directly to the liberation movements. While it is obvious that the ultimate recipients of this type of humanitarian aid will include both those who are politically militant and those who are not, the ultimate test of the value of this aid is the peaceful and humanitarian nature of the project itself.
This humanitarian aid goes to sponsoring bodies that have in mind medical, educational, agricultural and other humanitarian projects. Under this program, CIDA considers requests for contributions from reputable Canadian non-governmental organizations and international bodies for projects of a humanitarian nature in Namibia, Rhodesia and South Africa, (b) No, and it is not considering giving such support.
3. Revenue-Canada in its determination of what is and what is not charitable in the legal sense, relies heavily on common law established over a period of some 300 years. It has been held at law that if the purpose of a trust is the attainment of a political object, the purpose will not be charitable. The financial support of a liberation movement would be a political purpose and an organization engaged in this activity would not qualify for registration as a charitable organization with Revenue-Canada. A Canadian charitable organization may, on occasion, find it necessary to utilize the facilities of an organization outside of Canada to assist the Canadian organization to carry out its charitable activities outside of Canada. The intermediate organization may be a political organization but if the activity is charitable and is carried on in the name of the Canadian organization the activity normally would not be considered to be a political one. Revenue-Canada is seeking further information in regard to OXFAM-Canada dealings with a liberation movement in Africa.

The privileged information provisions of Section 14 of the Act specify that the Minister may not be required to disclose undertakings given by an investor where in the opinion of the Minister the disclosure of such undertakings would prejudicially affect the person who gave the undertaking in the matter of conduct of his business affairs. Accordingly, as a matter of policy and consistent with the Act, undertakings are only disclosed when and to the extent that such disclosure is not prejudicial to the business interests of the parties concerned. The Foreign Investment Review Agency monitors and reviews compliance by an investor with all undertakings, at appropriate intervals after allowance of the investment by Governor in Council. speechtext:
Insofar as the Foreign Investment Review Agency is concerned: 1. The privileged information provisions of Section 14 of the Act specify that the Minister may not be required to disclose undertakings given by an investor where in the opinion of the Minister the disclosure of such undertakings would prejudicially affect the person who gave the undertaking in the matter or conduct of his business affairs. Accordingly as a matter of policy, and consistent with the Act,

undertakings are only disclosed when and to the extent that such disclosure is not prejudicial to the business interests of the parties concerned. In such circumstances the undertakings are indicated in press releases issued by the Minister announcing the decisions of the Governor in Council with respect to the cases concerned. The Government is reviewing the nature and extent of the information that may properly be made public concerning proposed investments reviewed under the Foreign Investment Review Act. However, with respect to cases that have already been reviewed, the disclosure of information and undertakings given in confidence, and in the knowledge of the Government's existing practice and policy regarding disclosure, would be improper. The Foreign Investment Review Agency monitors and reviews compliance by an investor with all undertakings, at appropriate intervals after allowance of the investment by Governor in Council. As was indicated in the first Annual Report to Parliament on operations under the Foreign Investment Review Act, it is normally impractical to commence the monitoring process until approximately one year after allowance of the investment by the Governor in Council.
2. Public disclosure with respect to the specific business is not permitted under Subsection 14(1) of information obtained in the course of the administration of the Foreign Investment Review Act.

speechtext:
In so far as the Foreign Investment Review Agency is concerned: 1. The Foreign Investment Review Act was promulgated on December 12, 1973. Its first stage, namely, the acquisition of control of existing Canadian businesses by foreigners, was implemented on April 19, 1974; the second part, which prescribes the review of some categories of new enterprises established in Canada by foreigners, was implemented on October 15, 1975. The purpose of this law is to ensure that the acquisition of Canadian businesses and the creation of new Canadian enterprises by foreign Companies would result in significant advantages for Canada. speechtext:

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEVELOP EFFECTIVE ENERGY STRATEGY FOR ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is imperative, if we are to have an energy policy, for Canada, that it is a policy for all Canadians and not just western Canada or, indeed, central Canada.
The policy document "An Energy Strategy for Canada" presented an opportunity that has been sadly wasted-the chance to take leadership on the Atlantic power issue. In 23 pages of policy recommendations, Atlantic Canada was mentioned only eight times. No new policies were announced which will answer the special problems the region faces. Moreover, the policy of moving to world prices, aside from whatever other benefits may accrue, will certainly put a heavy strain on already fragile economies, the Atlantic region, consuming 40 barrels of oil per capita, uses a third more oil per head than Quebec, the next largest consumer. Half of the region's electricity is oil-fired.
Even with subsidies, the escalation of oil prices in the past two years has created real hardship. In Nova Scotia, electricy prices have risen by approximately 70 per cent in one year. There is only a vague reference to the problem in the report, as follows:
-(the government will be) encouraging substitution of electricity generated from domestic energy resources, including hydro and coal, for electricity generated from imported oil.
Beyond this the government has nothing to say about this crucial problem. The people of the Atlantic provinces do not want jam tomorrow; they want leadership today. The arrogance of this government is summed up by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie)

May 4, 1976
Energy
who seems to believe that what benefits central Canada is in the national interest, but what harms Atlantic Canada harms that area alone. The federal government offers no special assistance of any kind to alleviate the region's pressing problems. To date, the principal forms of aid offered by the federal government have been grants to cover 50 per cent of the cost of nuclear power stations, grants to cover half the cost of regional interconnections between provinces, and Fundy tidal power studies, but nothing has been done to help alleviate the problems-and it is obvious from ministerial pronouncements that nothing will be done.
The federal policy of giving grants to cover half the cost of the first nuclear station purchase by a province is not motivated by any compassion for the east coast's energy problems, but is simply a loss leader for nuclear sales. Aside from considerable doubt about the safety of nuclear power stations, their reliability and the hazards of waste disposal, the economics of nuclear power are coming into serious question. Last month it was announced that the anticipated costs of the New Brunswick nuclear power station had increased by $100 million to $600 million, an increase of 20 per cent. The net result is this: at present coal prices of about $30 per ton delivered, nuclear and coal-fired electricity cost about the same.
Despite not knowing what the impact of nuclear generating will be, the government insists on going ahead with nuclear generators. Would it not be a great deal better for the provinces concerned if the construction of coal-fired electricity plants was encouraged, thus avoiding the problems associated with nuclear power and encouraging the growth of an indigenous coal industry.
An examination of the proposal for research and development as it affects Atlantic Canada shows that it is totally inadequate for meeting the needs of the Atlantic provinces. The policy document spells out exactly where the special research and development needs of the Atlantic provinces are as far as federal research funding priorities are concerned-namely, at the end of the line. Renewable energy, which includes as its biggest component the Fundy tidal power scheme, is second to last in terms of federal priorities. Transmission system research ranked last. But transmission systems are of vital importance to the Atlantic provinces if the full benefit is to be derived from a regional or national grid. Transmission losses from ordinary power lines over long distances are substantial. Research taking place at the moment indicates that supercooled conductors could reduce power losses almost to zero. Yet the federal government put research and development in this area at the very bottom of the list. Another area of research taking place in Britain is in wave power. Preliminary findings indicate that more power generators may well be economic at current oil prices and could generate a significant proportion of base load electricity in the Atlantic provinces. Yet the government has neglected this area entirely.
It could be said that the Nova Scotia power crisis is partly the fault of the province's Liberal government. Nova Scotia, as a province, is hit hard. It is to some extent a victim of the provincial government's own energy policy. Following the provincial takeover of the industry, Nova

Scotians were subjected to a barrage of advertising designed to encourage the growth of all electric heating. There was substantial response: some areas, such as new developments in Halifax's Sackville suburb, are virtually all electrically heated. Home owners now pay as much as $350 in power costs every two months during the winter. In a significant number of cases, individuals have had to sell their homes because of power costs.
We now need some scheme in the Atlantic provinces which will encourage home owners whose principal residence is electrically heated to convert to more efficient fossil fuel fired heating systems which should take the place of their electrical heating systems. A given quantity of heat in an electrically heated home in Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island requires three times as much oil as the same home would require if heated with an oil furnace. In addition, great strides have been made in coal fired central heating in Europe. Some of this technology could be applied in the Atlantic provinces.
In summary, my party believes that an adequate energy policy for Canada must include a positive program for dealing with the high cost of fuel which the people of Atlantic Canada must pay. We do not think that the policy of continuing to support the Atlantic provinces' energy costs with the type of subsidy which has been paid in the past is viable. We think it essential that the federal government should take strong action in research and development so that the Atlantic provinces can use their potential energy resources for the generation of power. That part of the country should not be dependant on changes in price governed by OPEC countries. It should not be the victims of the federal government's insatiable need for tax revenues. Its energy program should be indigenous, using the resources of the area so that the people of Atlantic Canada may have energy at prices appropriate to their incomes.
It was totally unacceptable for the minister to bring down a report on energy strategy for Canada which ignores totally the substantial needs of the people of Atlantic Canada. In the report, the government showed, again, that it is interested in technology and techniques but is not at all interested in people. The report should have dealt with an energy policy for all Canadians. It ought to have evaluated what the people of Canada, of all regions, need- not just of the west, of the central part or of the eastern region. But it did not do this. Also, this report does nothing at all for the people of Atlantic Canada.
We ask the government to reconsider what it is doing in research and development, to reconsider its priorities, to reconsider its proposals for nuclear energy and to provide realistically for the energy needs of Atlantic Canada. We ask it to develop an energy program which will meet the needs, not in 15 years, not in 10 years, but immediately. The government is responsible for developing a realistic energy program for Atlantic Canada. We must move in that direction. The purpose of the opposition motion today is to bring to the attention of the government as forcefully as possible the need for responding to the energy requirements of the people in an important part of this nation, namely, in the Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEVELOP EFFECTIVE ENERGY STRATEGY FOR ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) for introducing the important topic of energy
May 4, 1976

on a Tory opposition day. Nova Scotia now has the dubious distinction of having the second highest power rates in Canada, next to Prince Edward Island. These rates, combined, are now about double the national average, Nova Scotia being some 27 per cent above the national average.
Let us briefly summarize our position from the point of view of power sources and our position relative to other Canadian provinces. Prince Edward Island uses oil for 100 per cent of its generating capacity. New Brunswick generates about 40 per cent of its power from oil, 50 per cent from hydro and 10 per cent from coal. Nova Scotia depends on oil for 70 per cent of its requirements, on coal for 16 per cent, which is contractually tied to the price of oil, and on hydro for 14 per cent. Newfoundland and Quebec derive between 90 per cent and 95 per cent from hydro sources. Ontario derives about 50 per cent of its energy from hydro, but also has a substantial nuclear base and depends on United States coal as well to fuel thermal stations. United States coal used by Ontario has increased but has not gone up at the same percentage rate as oil in the Atlantic region.
The western provinces have substantial hydro generation in their systems. Their thermal operations use coal, in most cases from their own leases, which is provided through what the English call open cast mining and which we usually call strip mining. The price of coal there is less than $5 per ton.
In early 1974 the Canadian wellhead price of oil was $3.80 per barrel. It rose to $6.50 and on July 1, 1975, to $8. We know that very likely it will rise to $9.50 or $10 per barrel by July. The federal government is pursuing its goal of allowing the producing provinces to go to parity with the world monopoly price established by the OPEC cartel. Meanwhile, oil which in 1971 was brought from Venezuela and the Middle East to the east coast for less than $2 per barrel now costs more than $13 delivered by tanker from the same two sources.
The federal government estimates that for the fiscal year 1976-77 it will cost some $1.41 billion in subsidy payments to make up for the difference between the Canadian and the world price. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), when replying to a question of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forre-stall) on April 27, 1976, as reported on page 12915 of Hansard, misled the House, I think, when he said:
The numbers I have seen indicate that very close to $1 billion has been paid indirectly to the consumers of Atlantic Canada as a result of the compensation program; that is, very close to $1 billion will have been paid to them by this summer.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Trudel), when he used the figures for compensation payments in the House on March 16 in replying to me, used the figure quoted earlier of $1.41 billion for the 1976-77 fiscal year as referring to all the territory east of the Ottawa Valley line. This means that anywhere from two-thirds to 75 per cent of the total compensation payment was going to the province of Quebec. On that premise, I conclude the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources misled us, perhaps inadvertently, on the compensation payments made to the Atlantic region.
Energy
Last year, power rates in Nova Scotia increased by 50 per cent. As every member from Nova Scotia knows, there have been citizen protest meetings held all over the province. Now, if we assume an increase by July 1 of $2 a barrel, the province's power rates are estimated to increase by an additional 10 per cent. However, that is not the end of the story for Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotia Power Corporation gets about one-half of its heavy fuel oil from Imperial Oil. A long-term contract with that company expires at the end of the year. We are purchasing that oil now at $1.75 a barrel. There will be another 20 per cent increase in our electrical costs when that contract expires. Incidentally, Imperial Oil has the Power Corporation before the courts on the interpretation of this contract which, if the Power Corporation loses, could cost the province another $100 million more or less.
In any case, Nova Scotians are faced with a maximum increase of 100 per cent in cost over a two-year period. In a have-not province, these are formidable obstacles to development, even with a special federal government subsidy which cabinet members who have spoken so far seem to frown on. It is estimated that it would take a total subsidy of $15 million to $16 million to bring Nova Scotia's electrical costs in line with the Canadian average.
The fuel bill for the Nova Scotia Power Corporation in the fiscal period which began April 1 is forecast to be $85 million. On the basis of 1972 oil prices, this would have been $20 million to $25 million. This I submit, Mr. Speaker, is a valid indicator of the extra burden now being shouldered by Nova Scotians and Prince Edward Islanders and, to a lesser extent, citizens of New Brunswick and Newfoundland. With the exception of Ontario, where imported coal from the U.S. would have a much less significant impact, this unfair situation applies to no other electric consumers in Canada outside of the Atlantic region.
Some of Ottawa's energy planners have, through the press, suggested that the present Liberal government in Halifax has brought the trouble upon its own head. The reference by the hon. member for Don Valley to electrical heating that was promoted by the Nova Scotia Power Corporation is, in my opinion, valid. I hold no brief for the government in Halifax, especially since they, along with the Tory government which ran the province before them, badly messed up the redevelopment and modernization of the vitally important steel plant in Sydney. However, I find it difficult to fault Nova Scotia's claim that they were led down the garden path on power costs by the federal government.
It is a fact that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), who was then minister of energy, mines and resources, in 1973 tabled a document in this House entitled "An Energy Policy for Canada". That document projected that foreign oil would be less than $4 per barrel by 1976 and would not reach $7 per barrel until the year 2000. On March 30, in response to a question of mine, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, said that they offered Nova Scotia the opportunity to participate in a regional nuclear reactor. He went on to say: "That offer was not taken up." As I understand it, that offer was one of a loan, or loans, to help build a second nuclear reactor at New Brunswick's Point Lepreau nuclear complex which is slated to be on-stream by 1980. The last estimate that I saw

May 4, 1976
Energy
for the Lepreau plant amounted to $650 million. That was a couple of years ago. I understand-and maybe the minister can give us a better figure-it is now estimated to cost well over $1 billion.
The power officials in Nova Scotia said they would not take part in the Lepreau complex because they could not get a guarantee on the price power and they were concerned about escalating capital costs over which Nova Scotia would have no control. They also argued that Nova Scotia would not get any economic spin-off if the plant were built in another province, and from their point of view it would be unsound to get a large block of power from a single source susceptible to breakdowns in an electrical system as isolated as that of Nova Scotia. I doubt whether the minister can claim that nuclear-powered electricity will be cheap at the New Brunswick plant. The experience of these plants in the United States has not shown that to be so. In fact, nuclear costs keep rising at a great rate.
Ottawa claims that its other offer was to pick up 50 per cent of the tab for the study of a regional power grid, plus 50 per cent of the capital cost. The Nova Scotia government denies flatly that they ever refused that offer. In fact, the Premier of Nova Scotia tabled a submission in the Nova Scotia House recently showing that is 1971 the Nova Scotia Power Commission, as a member of the maritime power pool, made an offer to the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion for assistance toward an accelerated generating transmission program between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. No federal action was taken on that submission.
A regional power grid involving the five eastern provinces would be helpful, but it requires the co-operation of all provinces and it seems that they have not been eager to go ahead. In fact, New Brunswick has given notice that it will charge what the market will bear for any electricity crossing its territory between Labrador, Quebec and Nova Scotia. It was at Nova Scotia's suggestion that the interprovincial advisory council on energy was established in late 1974. Last September, on the initiative of Premier Bourassa of Quebec, the premiers of the five eastern provinces agreed to a study to determine the availability and the economics of transmitting any surplus power. The manager of the Nova Scotia Power Corporation, Mr. Kirkpatrick, told the industry committee of the Nova Scotia legislature at the end of March that the preliminary report was not optimistic. It appears that there will be no surplus power from Quebec or Labrador in the near future. Every indication points to the fact that the regional power grid would not bring in cheap power from Nova Scotia.
I was glad to see, in the minister's submission last week, the renewed effort to get the Fundy tides studied again, but I think we have to be realistic on this score and realize that if this is going to be a steady power contributor, rather than one depending on the peaks of the tide, it will be extremely expensive and very capital-intensive. What the government of Nova Scotia should do is open two additional coal mines in the Cape Breton area, one at Lingan on the Phalen seam, and one at Donkin, which was recommended in 1971 after the closure of No. 2 mine in Glace Bay by the then special adviser on coal to the federal government, Mr. Alex Brown.

I think that in terms of British thermal units, one ton of coal is equated to four barrels of oil. The usual estimate for Cape Breton coal is 26 million Btu's per ton; for one barrel of oil it is six million Btu's. If oil is to cost the Power Corporation of Nova Scotia between $15 and $17 a barrel by 1980, then surely, given the high rate of unemployment in Cape Breton and the diseconomies which come from depending on buying nuclear power from New Brunswick or obtaining cheaper power from the regional grid, the province should return to coal to provide a great deal of its thermal needs, although we must admit that up to now the reserves capable of being mined are not accurately known. However, Devco intends to carry on an active program of offshore drilling.
Of course, it takes time and money to open new coal mines and the only answer to the short run problem of Nova Scotia from now until 1982 is a special subsidy or special equalization grant from the federal government to keep that have-not province from becoming even worse off economically. If we neglect to do this, not only will development be hindered but many pensioners and others in low income groups will face an unbelievably cruel situation as human beings and as citizens of this nation.

I do not think the minister is anxious to make a speech, in view of what he has been saying today and what he has said in the past. Regardless of what they believe the approach to this problem should be, every one has to agree that the maritime provinces, especially Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, are confronted by an alarming prospect. Whether a solution is difficult or whether it is reasonably within everybody's grasp, one gets the impression here in the House that the minister and the government are not really sympathetic in terms of finding an approach to this problem.
There can be no question about the prospect in store for a good many individuals, some of whom are obliged to get along on low incomes. In any event, I assume the government of Nova Scotia will have to show some leadership, hopefully in association with the government here, in finding some way of alleviating the conditions in which those individuals find themselves.
I want to take the limited amount of time available to me today to talk about the effect of higher increased fuel costs, both the increase which has already taken place and the increase which is to be expected, on the economy of the
May 4, 1976

region. In doing so, I do not in any way play down the effect of those increases upon individuals, but I am concerned this afternoon to place before the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie)-who is in the House and who is the responsible minister-the effect of those increases in power costs upon the government's whole program for fighting regional disparity in the maritime provinces. This is a subject in which the minister responsible for DREE should have an intense interest.
Fighting regional disparity has been an important aspect of government policy during the lifetime of the administration under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and, indeed, prior to that time. The results have not been particularly sensational, but the government has made this a priority and certainly it has spent a good deal of the taxpayers' money in an effort to reduce regional disparity by encouraging the development of the maritime economy. Ever since 1968, the year in which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established, I have contended that one of the great weaknesses of the government's program of regional economic development has been the lack of co-ordination within the government of Canada itself. The minister responsible for DREE would take some initiative which would be helpful, only to find it counterbalanced by action taken, for example, by the Minister of Transport.
Today we are discussing a striking example of a development which will clearly undermine the efforts of DREE to develop the economy of the maritime provinces generally. I do not want to be unfair to the minister, but in my opinion he, as the minister responsible, has shown a most cavalier attitude toward this whole question. I am not referring to the minister responsible for DREE, but to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Here is a striking example of a development which is taking place and threatening to escalate, one which is most discouraging to the development of industry in the eastern provinces. It affords a striking example of lack of co-ordination in terms of government effort.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said in the House the other day that the government of Canada is not likely to get into the business of equalizing power rates across the country. I accept that statement, but I have to ask the question: What will be the economic consequences of what is taking place with respect to power costs in the Atlantic provinces? What is likely to be the effect of increases in power costs on the movement of the economy in those provinces? Is it possible to develop some answer, if only a partial answer, which will not have the effect of offsetting any forward thrust which has been generated by DREE, by the provinces or by the people themselves? Is it possible to develop such an approach, rather than simply taking the attitude the minister seems to have taken, that the government of Canada has already done a great deal for the people of the maritime provinces, and let it go at that?
I accept the minister's point that a good deal of money has been spent in terms of tax-sharing and equalization. But I would ask the minister: What is the sense in the government of Canada involving itself in the kind of expenditure about which the minister has boasted, and
Energy
then letting the effects of all this go down the drain by allowing an increase in power rates? Let us give the minister and his government whatever credit they may seek for equalization payments and other special programs; but if they accept that credit then they must explain to the people, not only of the maritime provinces but of Canada why, having embarked on those programs, why they are sitting back coolly and allowing to happen what is happening to power rates while permitting the price of oil to move up toward world prices.
The minister and other spokesmen for the government have inferred from time to time that there are solutions available to the province of Nova Scotia, but they try to leave the impression that somehow the government of the province of Nova Scotia, or somebody down there, did not take advantage of the wisdom handed out in various emanations from the federal government from time to time.
What are the alternatives in Nova Scotia, for example, to the development of power from oil? There is the possibility of a switch to coal. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and my distinguished colleague from Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) of the NDP spoke about this. I should like to think that there is some prospect of a significant increase in the use of Nova Scotia coal in the development of power, but this would represent a substantial investment that would take a fair amount of time. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond understands all too well that we do not open a coal mine, for example, in six months, a year or even two years. It takes time.
I want to be frank with the House, Mr. Speaker. How much would a switch to coal really reduce the cost of power in Nova Scotia? I think it is an excellent idea in that it would involve additional employment in Nova Scotia and would add to the economy of the coal mining areas there. But I rather suspect that the price of coal from the mines would tend to follow upward the price of oil. I see the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond nodding his head in agreement. So that I am not misunderstood, certainly I favour the use of coal in the development of power in Nova Scotia, but I doubt very much whether, in terms of Btu's, over the years, coal would be a cheaper source of electrical power than oil. I gather from his nod that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond tends to agree that that is probably the case, though like me he has indicated that he favours the use of coal for this purpose in view of the development and employment opportunities involved. In any event, any movement in that direction would take time.
Federal ministers have also talked about development of an interprovincial grid. That, too, takes time. Recent inquiries have indicated that there is not likely to be any power available from sources outside the maritime provinces for a good number of years. There is no reason to believe that if a grid could be constructed, even within six months, it would result in the availability of cheaper power for Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. There is absolutely no indication that any such power would be available from Quebec, Newfoundland or Labrador for many years to come.
Another alternative is nuclear power. The station in New
Brunswick, I understand, will not be finished until 1980.
But how much is this power going to cost? For the sake of

May 4, 1976
Energy
New Brunswick, I hope it is not going to cost too much. I doubt that we will get any firm indication today from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources of what will be the cost of power generated by that nuclear power station. If the minister and his colleagues are going to talk to the House about sources of power other than oil, and are going to push nuclear power in Canada and its use in the maritime provinces, then they should be prepared to give us some pretty firm prices.
If these ministers are going to suggest to members of parliament in this country that this source of power constitutes an alternative-leaving aside for the moment any questions of safety in the CANDU system-and if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is going to suggest to the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island that they should turn to nuclear power, then they have to be able to give some pretty firm assurances as to cost, and I do not think they can do so. So I suggest that some of these alternative sources are pretty dubious. It seems difficult to put a firm cost on nuclear power.
Access to cheaper power through a grid seems to be based on the assumption that cheaper power from somewhere else is available, whereas in fact inquiries reveal there is no such power available, at least for quite a number of years into the future, if then. Where does that leave us, Mr. Speaker? I think it leaves the government of Canada in the position where it will have to stop talking in general terms and get down to actual cases. The government was told in the House today that there is no power available in the future under a grid system. Use of nuclear power has been questioned on the basis of how much it is going to cost. Is it going to be any cheaper than power generated by oil, even with oil at world prices?
I do not want to talk too long, Mr. Speaker, but may I just say that these alternatives will take years to develop. I do not think it is any exaggeration to say that it will take ten years to bring about any significant change in the cost of electric power in Nova Scotia by turning to an interprovincial grid or to nuclear power to any extent. I should like the minister, as well as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), to indicate to the House what they think is going to happen to industry of all kinds in the maritime provinces during that ten-year period. I think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should get together with the power authority down there with a view to working out a longer term solution which would hold together, not just generalities such as they have cast out to date. Certainly that is part of the answer. Part of the answer is for the responsible minister in the federal government to work out a longer term solution with the maritime provinces. They have not done that yet, at least I do not see any sign that the minister has put forward concrete, hard-headed alternatives to the way in which power is presently being developed there, unless one wants to talk about coal.
I ask my colleagues opposite what will happen to the economic development of the maritime provinces during the ten-year period when they switch to an alternative which the government of Canada has not yet developed. Does it make any sense to have embarked upon a program

of regional economic development in that area and let all else go down the drain by simply sitting back and refusing to work out some kind of interim solution?
I was amazed, in the committee on regional development, to find that the department has not had any study made of the effects of the anticipated higher power costs on the economic development of those provinces. They can ascertain very easily what the projections are about power rates. The Nova Scotia Power Corporation and the authorities in New Brunswick and in P.E.I. can tell the ministers what they expect the power rates will be, based upon changes in oil prices. But the responsible authorities in this government have not conducted any studies to ascertain what the effects of those high power rates will be on the economic development of the maritime provinces.
How can one possibly justify such a lack of interest? I do not pretend that the problem is easy to solve, but I cannot accept what seems to me to be the very cool, detached, cavalier attitude of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to this problem. I do not want to be unfair to the minister. I do not think it makes sense for the government of Canada, having involved itself deeply in a program of regional economic expansion, to refuse now to attempt to work out a selective and transitional program which will enable the economy of those provinces to continue to move forward.

I would be pleased to answer questions at the end of my remarks. The second problem is that of dilution. Every increase in the price of oil will have a greater effect on Nova Scotia and P.E.I. than elsewhere because of the higher proportion of their electrical energy which is generated from oil. The net effect of these two factors, lower efficiency and greater dependance on oil, is the real problem as far as the increase in electrical energy costs in Atlantic Canada is concerned, particularly with respect to Nova Scotia and P.E.I.
There are several other problems which I think are important to place on the record at the present time. One has to do with the rate of change of electrical energy costs. The Nova Scotia government did not increase the price of electrical power between 1958 and 1974, a period of 16 years. During that period most of the public utilities of the other provinces were moving the cost of their power up, so that their consumers were becoming adjusted to higher power rates. The Nova Scotia Power Commission, on the other hand, waited a full year and a half after the oil price increase before it moved its price up. Subsequently, of course, it had to move it up very much more dramatically, with all that that entails for the people and the squeeze on their incomes. Perhaps it might be worth noting that the real cost of electrical power today in Nova Scotia and in the Atlantic provinces, when compared with the average hourly wage of Nova Scotians and those in the Atlantic area, is lower today than it was ten years ago. To put it another way, wages have increased much more rapidly than power costs over that ten-year period, so that they have to work 35 per cent less time to purchase the same amount of electrical energy in 1976 compared with 1966.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recently proposed energy strategy for Canada tabled in this House by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) was received with great disappointment and some disillusionment in Atlantic Canada because the strategy does not seem to fully contemplate or to appreciate the severity of the impact of increasing electricity costs on consumers who live in an area which suffers from the effects of chronic regional disparity.
Hon. members may recall that people in Atlantic Canada, where wages in many cases are one-third below the national average, were among the first to feel the sharp edge of the government's anti-inflation program when the Irving firm dared to raise the wages of its employees above the guidelines. Some people in Atlantic Canada, particularly in the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, are facing electricity increases of 200 to 300 per cent and they have absolutely no hope of seeing wage increases to compensate for it. It is important that members of parliament from the Atlantic provinces make our colleagues in this House aware of this situation, and in my opinion it is imperative that any energy strategy for Canada should contain a thorough discussion of this situation if it is to be national in scope. Any attempt to ignore this problem or to avoid it is to tell maritimers to go back to the wood stove and furnace.
There is an uprecedented need for real statesmanship from our federal and provincial government leaders, and a greater need than ever for objective thinking and technical competence on the part of all professional people dealing with the short-term and long-term energy perspective. Compared with other nations, we are fortunate in that our problems are more in the nature of making choices between different energy sources and designing export poli-
May 4, 1976

cies in relation to surplus resources rather than of allocating supplies and rationing consumption.
In the field of energy development in Atlantic Canada, the federal government has not given the necessary leadership in developing, with the provinces, a master plan to provide a complete assessment and future development of the tremendous energy resources of Atlantic Canada which have been placed too far in the background in the minister's considerations and in his energy strategy. Without a full evaluation of the abundant hydroelectric and tidal resources of Atlantic Canada, the energy strategy for Canada and its policies for self-reliance are inadequate. The development of these resources for use in concert with other energy sources will provide an energy surplus for possible export at prices that can ameliorate the effect of accelerating fossil fuel costs.
One has to go no farther than the maritime provinces to see the sharp difference emerging in the cost of electrical energy produced in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, from basically a fossil fuel base, with the cost of electrical energy produced in New Brunswick where the development of hydro resources now in place has diluted the effect of fossil fuel increases. An energy strategy for Atlantic Canada must consider the combined uses of our four basic, potential energy sources. These are: nuclear, fossil fuels, the tides, and hydraulic resources.
The escalation of fossil fuel prices has placed a burden on economic development in the Atlantic provinces in general, and in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island in particular, to the extent that producers and manufacturers in these provinces have a very grim future indeed, and that future may very well be complicated by the existing restraint policies of this government.
I would like to outline some of the region's power resources. First, hydraulic resources. The major undeveloped water power resources of the Atlantic region total 38,130 gigawatts per hour annually. Of this amount, Newfoundland has some 36,000 gigawatts of undeveloped hydro potential, of which the Gull Island site on the Churchill River would produce 12,000 gigawatts, and Muskrat Falls 4,000 gigawatts per hour. The Saint John River in New Brunswick has an undeveloped potential of some 1,160 gigawatts in three sites. The 20 sites in Labrador amount to 35,000 gigawatts of the total potential. In addition, there are two sites in Newfoundland, five in New Brunswick, one principal site in Nova Scotia and miscellaneous smaller sites there. Of the five sites in New Brunswick, one contemplates the addition of units five and six to the Mactaquac dam site, and this is just about accomplished. The site in Nova Scotia that I was referring to is Wreck Cove in Cape Breton. This is under construction.
The maritime provinces coal reserves are set out in "An Energy Policy for Canada," volume 2, page 59. These indicate a total of 1,286,000 units of coal reserves measured in terms of thousands of short tons. Of this number, all but 10,000 units located in New Brunswick are in Nova Scotia. The price of coal in Nova Scotia has been tied to the price of oil and this has been a factor in the elevation of the price of coal. Obviously, coal will continue to make a major contribution to the generation of thermal power in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Most certainly, one worthy federal project is to inventory the lower grades of coal and
Energy
include in that peat moss and continue to support the modernization and mechanization of the coal industry in the maritimes. The gasification of coal and waste wood has reached a relatively high degree of technology and it, too, should be considered.
With regard to oil and gas, it is thought that most of Canada's ultimate potential for conventional oil remains to be discovered, with a large proportion of these resources being found in the frontier areas such as the continental shelves and the slopes of the Atlantic coast. Since 1959, some tens of millions of dollars have been spent there on geophysical surveys, and some hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on exploratory drilling. Over 200 million acres are now under permit.
The first offshore discovery was made by Mobil Oil on Sable Island in 1971, with significant oil and condensate finds. With 83 wells having been drilled, some would have been commercial discoveries had they been drilled on land, but with the high cost of collecting the oil and gas they will not likely come into commercial production until cheaper sources have been exhausted.
With regard to tidal power, the tides of the Bay of Fundy have, with possibly one or two exceptions, the greatest amplitude in the world. In Minas basin, the eastern branch of the upper bay, the maximum spring tide reaches an amplitude of 53 feet, and in Chignecto bay 46 feet. Thus, an immense volume of water moves in and out of these inlets every 12 hours and 25 minutes, which is the period of a tidal cycle governed by the rotation of the earth and its position relative to the moon and the sun.
Obviously, the energy contained in the moving mass of water is enormous. For centuries man has pondered way of recovering this energy. In recent years the problem has been studied in great detail. The dynamic and physical problems have been largely solved, and our technology and capital resources exist whereby there is no question of the capability of man to harness the tides. There are, however, a number of difficulties in the way of successfully and economically generating firm electrical energy from the tides. The first is the fluctuating nature of the tide, which means that in its present form there is no firm energy available except by adopting what is known as the two-basin scheme, which adds greatly to the capital cost of the structures. Thus, the form of processing or retiming involving additional generating facilities must be introduced before the tidal energy can serve a normal electrical power system.
A second difficulty lies in the magnitude of the structures and the problem of building these in what is essentially the open sea. The schemes which are being considered for the Bay of Fundy consist of dams across the inlets containing a large number of turbines connected to generators and a series of sluice gates. When the tide is rising, water flows through the gates and to some extent through the turbine openings into the basin formed by the dam. The basin can thus be filled to approximately the same level as that of the incoming tide. The gates and turbine passages are then closed and remain so until the tide has dropped sufficiently to create the head necessary to turn the turbines. The turbine intakes are then opened

May 4, 1976
Energy
and the water passes from the basin through the turbines and into the open bay. Thus, during every 24 hours and 15 minutes there are two periods of roughly four hours when generation takes place. There are many other arrangements of generation and filling cycles, but I shall not go into these as the one I have briefly described is the simplest.
Present studies indicate that the easiest site to develop on Minas basin would produce about 8,000 gigawatt hours per annum, and the two other most attractive sites on Chignecto bay could together produce about the same amount. Other arrangements might be found which would produce more energy. Studies carried out in 1967-1969 resulted in the conclusion that the cost of this energy was not competitive with that of other sources at the assumed interest rate of 7 per cent and considering the market price of fossil fuel at that time.
Subsequently, serious doubts have arisen as to whether these findings are applicable under conditions prevailing now. Retiming the tidal energy through hydro pumped storage or other means can serve the peak or middle range of the load demand. As such, it would be much more valuable than it would be as fuel replacement. Furthermore, with today's confused oil supply situation and current rates of inflation, a source of energy which once built can serve for decades at an assured cost is very tempting. Fossil fuel, nuclear and even hydro plants create some disruption of the environment. The environmental effects of a tidal development would be minimal.
The annual energy available from these principal sites that have been studied is just about equal to the total electrical energy consumption annually of the Atlantic region at the present time. It would provide for seven years' growth requirements of the region. To generate this energy in an oil-fired plant would require some 28 million barrels of oil a year.
Five potential pumped storage sites in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were examined in a preliminary way in 1968. The smaller sites of the order of 100 megawatts were found to have a cost of $90 to $130 per kilowatt at that time, excluding transmission, while sites of the order of 50 megawatts were estimated at $65 to $80. These sites will become particularly attractive for peaking purposes when nuclear plants are added to the system, with their low incremental energy costs. The pumped storage plants would also complement the development of tidal projects by upgrading the tidal energy from secondary to primary.
If nuclear power is used for load purposes, tidal power can be retimed to supply maximum and intermediate demands above the base load of an interconnected system. A power pool in eastern Canada involving the four Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec, with interconnections to central Canada and the United States, has tremendous potential for both the economic development of the region and the provision of power from renewable resources for all of Canada. This consideration should be heavily weighted in any energy strategy for Canada, but it is not mentioned in the paper presented to us.
The maritime electric utilities have made more progress in deriving benefits than interconnections and integration of their electrical systems and from interconnections with neighbouring regions than any other area of Canada. Since
[Mr. Howie.j
the action taken on October 17, 1973, by a number of Arab states, the whole world has suddenly become aware of the fact that drastic changes in our supply and use of energy, and no doubt changes in much of our social and economic structure, are a reality which must be faced. The era of cheap energy is passed. Every effort will be needed to conserve, especially, expendable fossil fuels.
We are told that oil and gas upon which our present society depends so greatly could be depleted within the next three decades if the ever-increasing rate of consumption is continued, and certainly the cost of these present basic energy sources will continue to increase at rates which will place further severe stress on our economic structure. It has been stated by most authorities that in the decades ahead the rate of consumption of oil and gas must decline drastically. However, the prospect is for a sixfold growth in the demand for electrical energy in the next three decades, and by the year 2000 some 50 per cent of Canada's increasing energy consumption will be in the form of electricity. In the future, our basic electrical energy supply will tend no doubt toward nuclear fuel generating plants, and the variable component of this massive electrical demand will be carried by such facilities as conventional hydro plants operating at low load factors, smaller existing thermal units and tidal power plants.
The maritime region is most fortunate in that there exists within its boundaries the largest tidal power potential in the world, a source of energy the cost of which, after being constructed, will not be affected by inflation. Another very important natural resource which the region possesses is the availability of large bodies of cold water which cannot ecologically be degraded by thermal pollution and which are essential to the nuclear or high load factor component of future integrated electrical systems.
The maritime region has a very great potential in meeting the energy needs of the region for the future at the lowest possible cost, and it is suggested that this challenge can only be effectively met by a very close co-operative and completely co-ordinated effort by all the Atlantic provinces and the government of Canada, and in giving leadership in this field the government of Canada has been more distinguished by its omissions than by its acts of commission.
In the longer term search for new energy options, the government places in the same category the feasibility of using renewable resources represented by solar, wind, tidal, geothermal and biomass techniques. From this one can infer that the foot-dragging which has marked the government's performance to date in regard to the Fundy tidal power potential will continue. The government has not learned the lesson that the New Democratic Party taught so effectively, namely, "tomorrow begins today". There is a real need to develop blocks of energy in excess of the immediate needs of the region and the necessity of integration with other power systems in regions of Canada and the United States. A great deal of mutual benefit has resulted from the existing transmission interconnections New Brunswick has with Nova Scotia, Quebec and New England.
The New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, for example, has demonstrated great leadership and courage in pioneering much activity which has lead to these benefits.
May 4, 1976

There is no doubt that these benefits will be shared by Prince Edward Island when the cable interconnection is completed. However, there seems no doubt that if the maritime region is to acquire full use of its natural advantages in supplying the electrical energy needs of its people, and at the same time meet the challenge created by the oil crisis and the magnitude of the future requirements, then, as emphasized before, it is essential that the federal government provide an imaginative plan and give leadership and work in co-operation with the provincial governments who own the assets that this nation needs so greatly.
The energy from the three tidal power sites would save Canada, in balance of payments, at least $3 billion each decade and would generate electrical energy to the equivalent of 28 million barrels of oil per year every year. The sooner the tidal projects are developed, the more likelihood of lower capital costs due to inflationary trends. Even if present and future contemplated studies are accelerated by a crash program, the lag time to in-service would likely be 12 to 15 years. Very lucrative markets now exist for surplus energy which would be developed over the immediate requirements of the region. This could provide a return on investment to the region and would certainly assist in the amortization of borrowed capital. Contracts for the sale of this surplus could also provide collateral for borrowing in the United States in particular.
Some of the major power generating facilities on the Columbia River were built and owned by small rural communities through the use of taxes and bonds and contracts for the sale of power. These avenues of financing the tidal projects warrant investigation and have not been mentioned in the so-called "Energy Strategy" paper. An energy strategy for Canada should treat as a priority the development of the great potential in Atlantic Canada so that the region can take giant strides forward in its battle against economic adversity and all Canadians can share in the benefits of these great resources. All we need is a government which has the wisdom and courage to undertake great tasks and perform great deeds. It is a pity we did not have it ten years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in indicating quite clearly that I support the motion presented by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). It should not be necessary for the House to spend time debating a motion of this type, but the philosophy behind the government's paper on energy seems to indicate that something happens to Canadians from parts of Canada other than the Atlantic provinces. Some of these people, particularly cabinet ministers, seem to be obsessed by the belief that Canada ends to the east at the St. Lawrence River. Believe you me, Mr. Speaker, it does not.
Let me remind the House, and in particular the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), that Canada started in the Atlantic provinces, the provinces by the sea where the natural energy is. The document called "An Energy Strategy for Canada" presented to the House by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources seems to be mainly dedicated to a solution of our oil problems, oil being a depleting resource. Little or no reference is made to the renewable resources in this country. In the maritime provinces, our seaside provinces, the good Lord has provided us with a natural, renewable resource. I refer to Fundy tidal power to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) has already referred. This power is, proportionately, cheaper than a barrel of oil.
For most of my adult life I have heard time and again of studies being undertaken of Fundy tidal power. Again this year I understand another study is being made. One of the consultants is also one of those who made a study as far back as 1946. The studies in 1946 concluded that the harnessing of Fundy tidal power was possible, feasible and practical. The Fundy tides are not only the highest in the world, but the strongest. Anyone who has watched them and observed their effect knows that this is true; you do not need a study to find that out, Mr. Speaker.
One study that I know of had to do with the erection of facilities in Shepody bay, one of the bays in the bay of Fundy, at the junction of the Petitcodiac and Memramcook Rivers. In 1946, harnessing the tides was considered possible. Owing to the way the tides flowed in that particular location, it was possible to get the benefit of them, not once or twice a day but four times a day; and there was provision for storing power. This sort of thing has been done successfully in European countries and I see no reason why Canada cannot do it in the maritime provinces.
Since the forties, some progress has been made in the Atlantic provinces in relieving regional disparity. In addi-

May 4, 1976
Energy
tion, since that time the federal government has seen fit to spend millions of dollars on the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway, even though this had a detrimental effect on the ports of Atlantic Canada.
The solid solution to the shortage of energy in the Atlantic provinces is the immediate development of tidal power. We need it now. There have been enough studies made of the question. It is essential that the federal government realize that the people of Atlantic Canada are as true blooded Canadians as those in any other part of this nation. We want to share in the progress of this nation along with the rest of Canada. We think we are part of confederation, yet when we read the document tabled by the minister we wonder if we are considered at all by those who prepared it.
In order to share in the growth of Canada, the people in the Atlantic provinces must be given greater attention by harnessing the power of the Fundy tides. I suggest that the minister of energy become more cognizant of what are the energy problems in Atlantic Canada. I take issue with the misleading conclusion reached by the minister today, though perhaps he did not intend to do so. He stated that the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission exported power to the state of Maine. That is true, but he did not indicate just how much power was imported by the province of New Brunswick through its electric power commission. As late as last night I was speaking to one of the ministers in the cabinet of the province of New Brunswick, and he told me that he believes imports and exports of power by the province of New Brunswick either balance or that the province is in a deficit position. This was not mentioned by the minister today.
The minister also made reference to insulation. I happen to be one of those in the maritime provinces who acted in response to the advertisements placed by all governments across the country for the installation of electric power. I put it in, but I put in the kind of insulation required by the power commission. There is a code and there are rules in the maritime provinces, and I suggest that the minister misled the House when he said there were no regulations. He also referred to speeding on highways. I contend that speeding in Ontario and other provinces in Canada is far more prevalent than in the maritime provinces. Our roads are not that good, Mr. Speaker.
There are several other items to which the minister and his department should direct their attention when it comes to providing electric power in Atlantic Canada. We need electric power immediately, and this energy is there. The good Lord put it there, and as minister responsible for energy, he can do something about it. An energy report of this nature so far as the maritime provinces is concerned is absolutely ridiculous.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to make a few brief comments on the motion before the House moved by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). It relates to the government's energy strategy paper which was introduced in the House last week. The motion makes particular reference to Atlantic Canada, whereas the document placed before the House last week refers to an over-all strategy for Canada. I think it is regrettable that the hon. member

for Don Valley did not make specific proposals for overcoming the increased cost of power in the maritime provinces, especially in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. He indicated that he would do so, but today he did not give any specifics when he spoke.
I was interested in the speech of the former leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who spoke about the regional development aspects of the problem. As a member who comes from a designated regional development area, I have great concern, along with him, for that particular aspect.
I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), when he spoke about the need for co-operation between the four Atlantic provinces and the federal government made an important point. This is really the key to solving the problem before the House today, especially the electrical power rates in the maritimes. This has been the approach that the federal government has taken through the years to the problem of providing assistance to provincial governments on a regional basis. Surely this is a region with special problems in that regard.
I want to refer briefly to the strategy paper, because it is important. I believe that all parts of it have significance for Atlantic Canada. The over-all plan laid out in the strategy paper is to reduce demand in the country through an active and aggressive energy conservation program and to balance this demand, which has been increasing at a rapid rate, with increased supplies of energy. Indeed, the paper foresees a reduction in the kind of growth of energy which we have had from 1970 to 1973 of about 5.7 per cent to about 3.5 per cent and perhaps much lower than that over the next ten years.
I think the government's program on conservation as introduced in February and as implemented now is very commendable. It has tackled the problems of the automobile. It has told auto manufacturers in this country that they must manufacture cars with an average fuel consumption of 24 miles to the gallon by 1980, and 33 miles to the gallon by 1985. It has indicated that the National Research Council has to produce a new set of minimum building standards for insulation which will be implemented by the end of this year either through a federal energy conservation bill or through provincial building code systems. It has provided an outline of minimum standards of energy efficiency for appliances, furnaces and home equipment. It has provided a proposal for the reduction of energy in industry.
Last month I had an opportunity to attend a conference of some 300 people from major industries across Canada which was attended by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand). It was interesting to see representatives from each sector of the economy outline how they would reduce, during the next six to ten years, energy consumption in their industries even though the industries are growing. Most of them indicated they would affect a 10 per cent to 15 per cent reduction in the energy consumption of the industry. The chemical industry, for instance, suggested they would be able to reduce their
May 4, 1976

consumption by some 11 million barrels of oil a year by 1980. The federal government, in its own in-house use of energy, uses a large percentage of energy in Canada and it has indicated that its target for this coming year will be a 10 per cent reduction of energy and that that level will be maintained during the next ten-year period. These are positive plans and proposals to reduce the increase in use of energy in this country to less than 3.5 per cent during the next ten years. A1 the same time, the paper outlined how we plan to increase the production of energy through exploration and development by doubling the exploration effort during the next three years in offshore areas and in the Arctic region to increase our supply of energy.
Likewise, the paper indicates that the pricing of our crude oil will move up during the next two to four years to world prices, not necessarily equalling world prices but approaching them. I think it is rather interesting that many of the newspapers in the country have extrapolated this figure to 25 cents a gallon increase. If we look at the price of oil, at $8.80 a barrel in the east, and the world price of around $13, we see a difference of $4.20. The figures given to me indicate that this would result in an increase in the cost of gasoline by some 12 to 15 cents a gallon, rather than 25 cents a gallon. By moving up toward the world price we would reduce the amount of compensation that has to be paid for oil imported from offshore to eastern Canada, we would increase the incentive for exploration and development, and the increased price would have a strong effect on conservation.
The paper also indicates there will be increased resource information so that companies exploring in the offshore areas or in the north, at least under federal jurisdiction, will have to make this information available earlier than they presently do, which will provide more information for the exploration of hydrocarbons.
The paper also indicates that interfuel substitution will be an important aspect of the strategy-the use of coal for gasification and to back up oil and natural gas, and the increased use of nuclear energy to save on oil and gas-fired thermalgenerating plants.
It also suggests that there be new delivery systems, whether they be pipelines from the Arctic, pipelines across Canada from Sarnia to Montreal, or other delivery systems which would be required with the new, increased use of western oil in Central Canada. It also talks about emergency preparedness. We are a member of the international agency, and we have responsibilities there. In the event of curtailment of energy supplies from offshore, there would be a sharing of shortages. This agency also provides us with an opportunity to exchange information on research and development in energy use. This is a very important aspect of that International Energy Agency.
Increased research and development is another point in the strategy. Our budget in the past year has been some $113 million. This will be increased during the coming year by some $10 million, which will put additional funds into the research and development programs for energy conservation, the policies which the hon. member for York-Sun-bury spoke about, increased studies in tidal energy and the other renewable resources of wind and wave action, as well as solar energy.
Energy
The last point in the strategy relates to increased Canadian content and participation in our energy programs through Petro-Canada and through the oil and gas regulations which will be tabled in the House later this year. If we look at the special problems of Atlantic Canada and their use of crude oil and fuel oil, whether for heating, gasoline or electrical generation, we find that during the past 2Vi years from January 1, 1974, to the end of June this year over $900 million will have been spent in subsidizing the crude oil used in Atlantic Canada, whether for use in automobiles, for heating or for electrical generation. This is part of our plan for one price oil and it gives Atlantic Canada a price which is competitive with other areas of our country.
Likewise, the coal which is used in Nova Scotia for thermal uses, whether for heating buildings or for use in generating electricity, has been indexed. The coal which is produced by the Cape Breton Development Corporation has been indexed to the price of crude oil. Up until the last couple of years the price of crude oil in the maritimes has always been lower than the oil coming from western Canada, and this coal has been indexed to the crude oil price. This amounts to a significant subsidy to Nova Scotia through the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
The problem is electrical energy. Prince Edward Island uses 100 per cent crude oil. Nova Scotia uses some 62 per cent of oil in generating its electrical power supply, and about 24 per cent is from coal. I have already indicated that both these commodities are presently subsidized by the federal government. In fact, for heating oil used for electrical generation about $120 million in subsidies has been paid or will have been paid between January 1, 1974, and June, 1976.
I think it would be well for hon. members to remember that the generation of electricity and the running of provincial electrical utilities is primarily under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and they jealously guard that jurisdiction. In fact, when considering matters of emergency before the Energy Supplies Allocation Board it was pointed out that the provincial governments have primary jurisdiction for the generation of electrical energy. However, in spite of this, I think it would be well to note that during the past decade or so the federal government has made significant contributions toward the generation of electricity in Atlantic Canada. These include the subsidies I already mentioned for the fuel used in electrical generation.
Under the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, loans of some $225 million were made, a grant for New Brunswick interconnection of some $4 million, a loan and grant for Prince Edward Island interconnection of some $27 million, a loan for the Point Lepreau nuclear plant of $350 million, an offer for the Gull Island transmission of some $343 million, grants for interconnection studies for P.E.I. and Newfoundland of $600,000, a grant for the tidal program from 1968 to 1969 of $1.6 million, and for the tidal study which is now taking place of $1.5 million, as well as Atlantic Development Board grants for electric projects of $55 million. This gives a total of $1,127.7 million which the federal government has contributed toward energy
13168

Energy
projects in Atlantic Canada and for the construction of these projects.
It would be well for us, also, to look at electrical rates across Canada. In March of this year the average rate across Canada was $23 per thousand kilowatt hours of electricity. By comparison, the Halifax rate at that time was $27.24 per thousand kilowatt hours. The Vancouver rate was almost $25-so they were both in the same ballpark. In the Ottawa area, the Kanata rate of Ontario Hydro is some $25.08 per thousand kilowatt hours. By comparison, the Charlottetown rate is higher, some $42 per thousand kilowatt hours. But I think we have to realize that all rates of electricity are going up in Canada. For instance, Ontario Hydro will be increasing its rate by some 22 per cent per year over the next five years. Manitoba Hydro has indicated that in April of this year its rate will be going up by some 28 per cent, and New Brunswick has indicated an increase of 12 per cent. So there are many areas in our country which have rates which at the present time are comparable with Halifax, and in practically every province these rates tend to be moving up.
I should also like to mention the exploration which will be taking place this year off the east coast under the auspices of Petro-Canada which will cost some $25 million in each of the next five years. This represents about 25 per cent of the budget of Petro-Canada. It is interesting to consider whether the official opposition, and especially those hon. members from Atlantic Canada, would support their leader's proposal to wind up Petro-Canada if the Conservatives ever were in power-which, of course, is very unlikely to happen for a very long time.
In reviewing some of the points I have made, I want to mention that Atlantic Canada does have some higher electrical rates, but coal rates and heating oil rates are comparable to other parts of Canada and those rates are subsidized by the federal government. The federal government has provided a great deal of assistance-almost $2 billion- over the last few years for electrical and other energy assistance to the maritime provinces. It intends to continue its assistance by providing for interconnections, the assistance I have already indicated as well as the assistance which it has already offered for nuclear plants in that area.
I think this is a strong indication of the kind of commitment the federal government has made, not only in the past but also in the future, to equalize opportunity in Canada and especially in Atlantic Canada.
